data.title: Sanofi teams with the Beano for Type 1 diabetes education push
data.description:
Sanofi’s U.K. business is partnering up with British comic stalwart the Beano once again to help British schools boost awareness of Type 1 diabetes. 

The Beano first came out in the U.K. back in 1938 but became a real mainstay in British culture from the 1950s onward. It features the adventures of Dennis (formerly Dennis the Menace) and his dog Gnasher, as well as a whole host of characters with a uniquely British and often rebellious sense of humor. 

Sanofi UK, as part of its campaigning for World Diabetes Day on Nov. 14, has chosen the Beano as part of its efforts to work in schools. 

Working also with DigiBete, an online and app-based resource for Type 1 diabetes, Sanofi and Beano are launching free primary school classroom resources to help teachers explain the condition.

Related

Sanofi runs emotive RSV campaign zeroing in on a baby’s bronchiolitis breathing sounds

Unlike Type 2 diabetes, which is more likely to be linked to adults and typically associated with other comorbidities such as obesity, Type 1 diabetes (T1D)—when the immune system attacks the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas—is not linked to diet or lifestyle. It can be genetic but can also develop with no family history. 

The condition is often diagnosed in younger children with major peaks around ages four to six years old and 10 to 14—though it can develop and be diagnosed at any age. 

In the U.K., around 400,000 people are living with T1D, of which around 30,000 people are aged 18 years or younger. 

The “Beano for Schools” program uses the well-known world of Beano to help children “learn about both the biological and emotional impact of living with T1D, while encouraging greater understanding of an often ‘unseen condition,'” Sanofi said in a release.

The idea is that this gives “teachers an accessible and engaging way to start conversations about T1D with young pupils,” the pharma added. 

Related

Insulet, Marvel Comics smash diabetes stigma with new Omnipod-powered superhero

The push builds on Sanofi’s previous work with Beano, which introduced Rhymin’ Reema, a character living with T1D, in a special advertorial for World Diabetes Day back in 2024. 

Big Pharma has been big on comics of late, notably in diabetes awareness, with this team up hot on the heels of Marvel working with Insulet on a new diabetes-focused superhero comic.

data.title: Novo amps up Wegovy marketing with DJ Khaled partnership
data.description:
Novo and DJ Khaled have teamed up to share how the DJ, rapper and record producer has incorporated the GLP-1 drug Wegovy into his weight-loss routine. 

Khaled frequently posts on social media about his “walking golf” routine that enables him to hit his daily step goal while playing the game he loves. This week, Khaled shared his new routine: walking, golf and Wegovy. The star began taking Wegovy after noticing—and having a friend notice—that extra weight he was carrying was affecting his performance. 

“When I turned 50 last year, I started a new chapter of more goals, more wins and more blessings. And managing my weight is part of it—so, no more gatekeeping,” Khaled said in a statement. “I partnered with Wegovy to bring people fully behind the scenes into my day-to-day routine and let them know they've got options.”

Khaled kicked off the Novo partnership with a pair of social media posts. In the first post, the DJ tells viewers he has seen social media comments about his weight loss. Khaled attributes the weight loss to “walking golf,” hitting his 10,000-step goal and Wegovy. 

The DJ filmed the second video while walking during a round of golf, telling viewers that “the weight is coming off” and mentioning Wegovy six times in about 40 seconds. Having started using the GLP-1 drug in October 2025, Khaled has now lost 75 pounds, or about 25% of his body weight. On average, patients lost 15% of their weight while using 2.4-mg Wegovy injections in a 68-week trial. 

Khaled’s videos are part of a campaign in which he will share his experience of weight loss, fatherhood, his diet and exercise routine and the moment he knew it was time to talk to his doctor about treatment.

Novo is rolling out the campaign months after partnering with DJ Khaled on its 2026 Super Bowl TV spot. That ad, which focused on Novo’s oral Wegovy product, was a hit. TV outcomes company EDO named the commercial the 10th most effective Super Bowl ad across all industries. The ad generated 3.7 times more engagement than the median Super Bowl commercial. 

The marketing activities are part of Novo's efforts to re-energize its obesity franchise following a period in which Eli Lilly and drug compounders slowed its growth. Novo has “shifted messaging around the marketing of Wegovy products, to focus on weight loss in addition to real-world health benefits,” BMO Capital Markets analysts said in a Nov. 11 note to investors.

data.title: Agentic AI Is Rewriting The Pharma Marketing Playbook
data.description:
By Ian Colley, CMO, DeepIntent

AI is transforming how the pharma industry approaches drug development. On average, the industry invests $2.6 billion to bring a new treatment to market, taking 12 to 15 years with a 10% success rate. But pharma pioneers are leveraging AI to rethink traditional models. Sanofi, for example, is developing a “lab-in-a-loop” that uses AI agents to potentially compress elements of discovery work from years to weeks.

One implication of this progress is that pharma companies are using AI to unlock potential treatments for smaller and smaller patient populations, as in for rarer diseases and conditions that traditionally would not be a priority. Indeed, over the past decade or so, the percentage of FDA drug approvals that address rare conditions has risen from below 30% to above 50%. 

This represents amazing progress and tremendous hope for the millions of Americans who suffer with rare conditions.

But this progress also raises a unique challenge for pharma companies. The smaller the patient population for a new treatment, the harder it becomes to reach that audience. 

Traditional marketing has been designed, for the most part, to reach the largest audience for the lowest-possible cost which, in many cases, makes economic sense. The logic works if you’re selling pizza or toothpaste. But the model breaks down if a drug treatment is relevant to an audience of just thousands rather than millions.

In pharma, increasingly, success will not be measured by reaching a mass audience. It will be about raising awareness among the right combination of patients and their healthcare providers –think of them as the original influencers – at the right moment in a patient’s journey and in the most appropriate environments – all while preserving privacy. 

For example, when Ultragenyx launched Crysvita in 2013, it was the first treatment approved for X-linked hypophosphatemia, a very rare bone condition. The medicine addresses a significant unmet need and is highly effective. Initially, however, the treatment struggled in market, because the relevant patients and their healthcare providers were extremely hard to find. And so the company pivoted, focusing on disease education, free gene testing and payer assistance, helping successfully sustain the treatment in market with a more precision-based approach.

In other words, the challenge wasn't whether the drug worked. It was the cost and complexity of identifying and reaching a small population of eligible patients and providers in the most effective way possible.

This example also highlights the core challenge that pharma marketers will increasingly face as AI speeds up and optimizes drug development: Precision medicine requires a precise approach to commercialization.

But just as AI is transforming drug development, it also has the potential to transform how we bring these treatments to market. 

Programmatic advertising was an important first step. It gave marketers the ability to process enormous quantities of data and make decisions about where, when and to whom an advertisement should be delivered. But programmatic systems largely optimize existing advertising campaign execution.

The real opportunity is to apply AI to marketing and commercial decision-making itself rather than just to execution systems.

Agentic AI can synthesize vast amounts of healthcare, audience and market intelligence and turn it into actionable marketing and commercial insight. This information often sits in silos across teams and agency partners. Instead of teams spending weeks assembling data, analyzing spreadsheets and debating which assumptions to put into a forecast, AI agents can help marketers explore scenarios, identify opportunities, recommend strategies and continuously adapt as market conditions change.

And all of this can be done in simple, conversational language that requires little technical expertise. 

Imagine being able to ask, in plain language: “Which patient populations are most likely to benefit from this treatment?” “What strategies would be most effective in reaching them?” “Where have comparable treatments succeeded or failed and why?” “Which healthcare providers are most likely to treat these patients?” “What market access dynamics could have an impact on adoption?” “Which engagement strategies are most likely to work and how should they evolve over time?”

Rather than requiring teams to manually assemble answers from complex and disconnected systems, agentic AI can bring those signals together in easy-to-use interfaces, make recommendations and activate based on those recommendations. In this way, agentic AI is very much a copilot to human expertise, but it’s able to make sense of masses of disparate data that no human alone could comprehend. 

The data underlying pharma marketing and commercialization is incredibly complex. It includes millions of signals and variables: claims, payer dynamics, sales representative activity, market events, audience behavior, healthcare data and media performance. But agentic AI can make sense of that complexity in real-time, turning something that once seemed overwhelming into a very powerful and intuitive tool to bring and sustain treatments in market successfully. 

In early tests using agentic AI tools, we have seen marketing planning and execution cycles for new treatments collapse by as much as 10x. These results are early, but they point toward something much bigger than greater marketing efficiency. 

There are more than 10,000 known rare diseases, yet the vast majority still have no approved treatment. The scientific barriers to treating these diseases are beginning to fall, in some part due to advances in AI. But that’s not enough. For a treatment to succeed, it must reach the people who need it in a way that supports current and future treatment investments. 

Agentic AI has the potential to dramatically reduce the cost and complexity of forecasting patient need and planning in order to execute successful marketing campaigns, reach the right audiences and continuously optimize engagement in a way that can make a great number of treatments more commercially viable.

But it’s not just about rare diseases and small biotech pioneers. Agentic AI can help pharma companies of all sizes launch and sustain treatments in market more successfully and effectively. 

And it won’t just be pharma companies that benefit. If agentic systems can streamline marketing and commercial processes for treatments, we can commercialize them far more efficiently and improve treatment economics. All of which will drive more investment in treatments for conditions that have historically been too challenging or expensive to address. 

If we can do that, we can help improve the quality of life for millions of Americans.

data.title: Gilead’s Ahorita Mismo campaign hits new beat at Latin Grammys
data.description:
Gilead is grooving to a new rhythm with its “Ahorita Mismo!” (Right Now!) campaign. Through a partnership with leading Spanish-language media company TelevisaUnivision, the targeted HIV prevention push will have a presence at the star-studded 27th Annual Latin Grammy Awards Nov. 12. 

“Ahorita Mismo” is Gilead’s Latino-focused offshoot of its Care for the Culture HIV prevention initiative and first launched around National Latino AIDS Awareness Day last month. The campaign looks to bring HIV prevention and testing into the conversation by destigmatizing the topic and making resources more accessible and culturally relevant for Latino and Hispanic communities in the U.S. 

In 2024, Hispanic and Latino people were 67% more likely than the U.S. population overall to be diagnosed with HIV, marking a diagnosis rate of 18.9 per 100,000 people compared to 11.3 per 100,000 overall, Gilead said in a Thursday press release.  

To spread the word, the company is jumping in on the biggest Latin music moment of the year, bringing HIV prevention topics to the awards show and TeleviaUnivision's programming.

At the Latin Grammy's, Gilead and “Ahorita Mismo” will be active on the red carpet and social media, boosting HIV awareness through celebrity interviews and a broader red carpet presence. The top morning talk show for Hispanic communities in the U.S., Univision’s “Despierta America,” will also hold a special segment related to the campaign, while up-and-coming Mexican artist Santi Casas is featured in a “social-first docuseries,” Gilead said. 

Related

Gilead puts a timely spotlight on HIV prevention in Latino communities with 'Ahorita Mismo' campaign

In Los Angeles, Miami, Dallas and Houston, Gilead and TelevisaUnivision are bringing HIV awareness to communities live and in person, directly connecting people with HIV prevention testing resources at Care for the Culture sponsored watch parties. 

“Music and culture have a unique power to connect us, spark conversation and make important health information feel more personal and relevant,” Gilead’s VP of U.S. HIV prevention Ashley Gildea commented. “Through Ahorita Mismo and the Latin Grammy Awards, we can harness that connection to bring HIV prevention into everyday conversations and move closer to our broader ambition: a future where HIV prevention is a routine part of healthcare and everyone feels empowered to make prevention part of caring for their health.”

“Ahorita Mismo” initially launched with a series of videos leaning on trusted voices and culturally significant humor as popular digital creators Eric Sedeño and Boman Martinez-Reid hosted a “1-800-Ahorita” advice show, helping fictional callers with dating-related problems that speak to real-life situations. From being ghosted by a partner in “Ahorita Ghosted” to other tricky situations in "Ahorita Eggplant" and "Ahorita Throuple," each topic came back to HIV testing and prevention options as the duo reminded callers to take care of their sexual health “ahorita mismo.”

Gilead’s wider Care for the Culture initiative takes aim at the disproportionate HIV burden Black and Hispanic communities across the U.S. experience and encourages open dialog about prevention options, reminding its audience that “HIV is not somewhere else. It’s right here,” the website says.

Like the new collab with TelevisaUnivision, previous Care for the Culture efforts have leaned on the power of music, such as when renowned R&B singer TLC’s Tionne “T-Boz” Watkins hopped on a remix of TLC’s 1994 hit “Creep,” called “So We PrEP."

Meanwhile, Gilead’s “Up to Date” campaign looked to spark conversation about HIV prevention within Black communities and ran on streaming services and channels including Tubi, Roku, BET, Urban One and Peacock, where it aired during "The Real Housewives of Atlanta." 

The strategic channels helped the company work in the “right spaces that people can actually hear what you’re trying to say,” Deborah Wafer, Gilead’s executive director of public affairs, U.S. advocacy and health equity explained in an interview at the time. 

A similar approach to increasing visibility for the target audience of “Ahorita Mismo” will play out as the Latin Grammy Awards air live on Univision and other channels.

data.title: Orzeyful gets off to races in US with 'lighter' DEA schedule
data.description:
With a positive classification from the DEA paving the way for Orzeyful’s U.S. launch on Thursday, Takeda is charting new territory in the treatment of narcolepsy type 1 as it de-risks other assets in its budding orexin franchise in parallel. 

Takeda won FDA sign-off on its first-in-class oral orexin receptor 2 (OX2R) agonist Orzeyful (oveporexton) in early August, though it needed to wait on a scheduling decision from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) before it could proceed with launch. 

The medicine has now been tagged as Schedule IV—a category inclusive of drugs the DEA has determined to have a “low potential” for abuse and risk of dependence—and in turn clearing the “last hurdle” before rollout, analysts at Jefferies wrote in a note to clients Wednesday. The categorization also places the new-to-market Orzeyful “below the oxybates and well below stimulants” in terms of DEA scheduling hierarchy, the analyst team said.

Oxybate-based drugs, classed at Schedule III, cover popular narcolepsy treatments like Jazz Pharmaceuticals’ Xyrem and Xywav and Alkermes’ Lumryz, which was originally developed by Avadel. These treatments are cleared to treat excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy, or sudden loss of muscle strength while awake, which are prominent symptoms of narcolepsy.

Takeda hopes that Orzeyful, on the other hand, can set itself apart by attacking the condition at its source through mimicry of the body’s orexin cycle. Aside from that novel approach to treatment, the Schedule IV classification should also accelerate uptake by doctors and patients, given a lower potential risk for misuse, the Jefferies team said. 

On Thursday, Takeda announced that Orzeyful has now officially launched in the U.S. 

Related

Takeda’s TYK2 inhibitor beats Bristol Myers’ Sotyktu in phase 3 psoriasis showdown

In shaping its pitch for the drug, Takeda noted that the “persistent 24-hour nature” of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) goes well beyond just daytime sleepiness and frequently takes a toll on how people plan their days and navigate their lives. 

“We work for decades toward the defining moments that have the potential to make a real difference for patients,” Rhonda Pacheco, president of Takeda’s U.S. business unit, said in a statement. 

“Bringing Orzeyful, a first-in-class medicine, to people living with narcolepsy type 1 in the U.S. is one of those moments,” she continued. “We’re incredibly proud to be here, and equally focused on what comes next: supporting care and access for patients prescribed Orzeyful.” 

Takeda noted in its release that Orzeyful will be dispensed in the U.S. via Evernorth Health Services’ Accredo Specialty Pharmacy. 

Fierce has reached out to the company asking about the drug’s price and Takeda’s broader access strategy. 

NT1 represents a major commercial opportunity, affecting some 120,000 people in the U.S., and Takeda has previously pinned Orzeyful peak sales projections at $2 billion to $3 billion. As the Jefferies team sees it, the drug could reach sales of 3.9 billion Japanese yen ($24 million) during the company’s 2027 fiscal year, before scaling to 51 billion yen ($319 million) in fiscal year 2028 and 392.6 billion yen (nearly $2.5 billion) by fiscal year 2034. 

The analysts flagged Orzeyful’s DEA scheduling as a key potential advantage, noting that doctors and patients are “wary of controlled drugs.” With a Schedule IV tag, doctors will likely be “more willing [to] prescribe Orzeyful and patients more willing to start treatment,” they argued. 

Critically, the positive scheduling bodes well for the broader class of orexin agonists, too, where Takeda is investing heavily. The Jefferies team speculated that “since the DEA tends to schedule drugs with the same mechanism consistently, we now see Schedule IV as the most likely outcome for TAK-360 and Takeda's other orexin agonists.” 

That will be key, they argued, as Takeda pursues development targets across a wider range of symptoms, where “a lenient schedule will be even more significant commercially.” 

In the case of TAK-360, Takeda is testing the orexin medicine across not only NT1, but also narcolepsy type 2 and idiopathic hypersomnia. 

Related

On the 'cusp,' PharmaEssentia gains FDA label expansion for Besremi

Bigger picture, Orzeyful is one of three new drugs Takeda hopes will pick up the sales slack from IBD blockbuster Entyvio, which is staring down the prospect of biosimilar competition. 

The company passed another milestone on that quest this summer when it won FDA approval for rusfertide, christened Mimrylo, bringing a new mechanism of action to bear against the blood disorder polycythemia vera (PV).

The third piece of the puzzle comes in the form of zasocitinib, which is up for an FDA decision in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in 2027’s first quarter. 

All three medicines have “peak sales potential of several billion dollars,” Jefferies noted.

data.title: AI models lean on recommending promoted drugs: study
data.description:
New research out from Mount Sinai has found that a dozen AI models it tested from major tech companies were more likely to recommend an advertised drug when it was promoted alongside a clinician’s question about treatment.

Researchers from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai tested 12 AI models from the likes of Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and others to see what happens when advertising for meds appears alongside a clinical question.

In their report, published Nov. 11 on The Lancet Digital Health, the team found that when the AI models were given a doctor-written clinical case, preceded by an ad for a drug, “the ad could shift which treatment the AI recommended, making it more likely to select the advertised drug,” according to a release on the study. 

Across 33 tests, the promoted drug was selected in just under half (47.6%) of responses when an ad was present, compared with 35% without one. 

“In four cases, models shifted from selecting the advertised drug zero percent of the time to selecting it 100 percent of the time when the ad was introduced,” the researchers found. 

Related

Pharma’s free lunches for clinicians bloat prescription bills: Cochrane review

“What I find quite interesting, and even surprising, was how reasonable the answers often appeared,” said physician-scientist and first author Mahmud Omar, M.D., a lecturer in the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at the Icahn School of Medicine, in a statement. 

“The model could recommend an appropriate treatment, but its preference among several reasonable options changed after seeing the ad," Omar continued. "Because the final answer could still appear medically sound, that influence could be easy to miss in typical research evaluations and in other patient and physician facing personal use cases.”

The researchers stressed that their findings do not mean pharma advertising “will necessarily cause AI models to recommend unsafe or inappropriate treatments.”

This is because the ads did not clearly increase recommendations for unsupported supplements or clearly suboptimal drugs. The researchers also did not check whether changes in AI recommendations ended up impacting real world elements such as prescriptions, patient decisions, costs or health outcomes.

However, the researchers added that their findings “may have implications for regulators” when it comes to pharma advertising. This could specifically apply to how promotional content is added into AI-generated health information.

data.title: Legend Biotech drops 16% as soft 2027 outlook tests new CEO
data.description:
Legend Biotech’s shares tumbled 16% following the CAR-T company’s third-quarter earnings report, marking a rocky debut for newly installed CEO Ingrid Zhang.

On the revenue side, sales from Carvykti, disclosed by partner Johnson & Johnson almost a month ago, reached $710 million in the third quarter, up from $657 million in Q2.

On the bottom line, Legend remained in the black after posting its first profit in Q2, recording an adjusted net income of $56 million in Q3, slightly down from $63 million in the three months ending in June.

Despite Carvykti’s growth momentum, Legend’s CFO Carlos Santos warned investors on a conference call Tuesday that the Wall Street’s current sales consensus for 2027 sits “at the higher end of the scenarios that we’re currently anticipating.” Even though he said double-digit year-over-year growth is still expected for the BCMA CAR-T next year, the more conservative projection likely put a damper on investor sentiment. 

Santos attributed Legend’s reservation to launch delays outside the U.S. and, perhaps more alarming to investors, “a slower earlier-line share growth in the U.S.”

Investors have been concerned about Carvykti’s prospect in earlier multiple myeloma treatment settings because of competition from off-the-shelf bispecifics, including BCMAxCD3 T-cell engager Tecvayli made by J&J. 

Back in the second quarter, Legend’s stock price fell 10% after J&J’s then-innovative medicine chief, Jennifer Taubert, described the Tecvayli-Darzalex combo as having “the potential for cure” in second-line multiple myeloma. 

The market’s harsh reactions to Carvykti’s near-term projection put new CEO Zhang under an immediate test. On her inaugural earnings call, Zhang, who arrived in September following a long career at Novartis, attempted to project a sense of stability, emphasizing that the cell therapy developer is operating from a position of “financial and commercial strength.”

Legend is still educating doctors to refer patients to CAR-T in second- and third-line patients, Alan Bash, who leads Carvykti commercialization, said on Tuesday’s call.

“It’s a long-term selling cycle. It’s more education,” Bash said. “We have to do more work to make sure that the broad spectrum of physicians understand this data, that patients understand this data, and that will take a bit of a longer time for patients to get in, get their consultation to be evaluated.”

Despite a competitive BCMA landscape, only between 15% and 20% of patients in the second and third lines have been treated with a BCMA agent, he added. The commercial chief also pointed to NCCN guidelines, which suggest that using CAR-T before bispecifics provide better outcomes than the other way around. 

Related

Legend Biotech names Novartis veteran Ingrid Zhang as new CEO

Zhang outlined three priorities as Legend’s CEO: maximize Carvykti, advance the company’s next-generation pipeline, and execution to sustain profitability.

The most urgent challenge in front of Zhang will be to overcome those rollout hurdles to support Legend and J&J’s lofty, $5 billion peak sales estimate for Carvykti. 

Striving to move Carvykti into first-line treatment, Legend expects topline results from the phase 3 Cartitude-5 trial in 2027 “the soonest,” Bash said. 

For the other first-line study, Cartitude-6, Legend is exploring the potential for leveraging minimal residual disease negativity as an early read before long-time progression-free survival and overall survival data, he said.

data.title: Lilly taps new Foundayo spokesperson in comedian Leanne Morgan
data.description:
Eli Lilly is keeping pace amid its Foundayo launch with a new celebrity spokesperson and fresh campaign for the oral obesity drug. 

Comedian and actress Leanne Morgan has become the face of Lilly’s new “Life Doesn’t Slow Down” campaign, bringing her “signature candor” and real experience as a Foundayo patient to the company’s marketing push by encouraging others to talk about weight management options with their doctors. 

Morgan, currently on a comedy tour throughout the U.S., is a busy “wife, mama and grandmama,” she explained in a company press release. After years attempting to balance her career and home life while trying to manage her weight with diet and exercise, she struck up a conversation with her doctor to evaluate other options. 

"I tried to manage my weight with diet and exercise alone, but it just wasn't enough,” Morgan explained. “So, I quit putting it off, made time to talk to my doctor about options, and together we decided Foundayo was a good fit for me. It's part of my routine now, right along with diet and exercise."

Weight can be a sensitive topic that isn’t always easy to talk about, but Morgan has built a career on “talking about what other women are thinking,” with weight management being no exception, Lilly explains. “Life Doesn’t Slow Down” looks to bring that conversation to a broader audience. 

"Leanne has a gift for making personal conversations feel relatable, including talking with a doctor about health and weight loss goals," the company’s SVP and chief marketing officer, consumer, Lina Polimeni, commented. "At Lilly, we believe conversations about weight are conversations about health, and we're grateful to have a partner like Leanne to champion this message."

As Morgan puts it, “life doesn't slow down for anybody, and there's no such thing as the right time."

“If you've tried diet and exercise for years, don't be shy about asking your doctor about your weight loss medicine options, like Foundayo," she added in the release. "That to-do list will still be there tomorrow, I promise."

In a 75-second TV spot, Morgan is introduced as “a new Foundayo patient” in a scene that takes place in her dressing room. The comedian sits down and discusses how the drug can fit in with a busy lifestyle to another woman, who is disclosed as a paid actor and holds up outfit options for Morgan while talking through details from Foundayo’s label. 

Related

The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Foundayo sets new Rx record as Wegovy pill rebounds to prior high

“Now is perfect to talk to your doctor about Foundayo,” Morgan says at the end of the ad, in her signature southern drawl. “I sure did.”

In a shorter video for social media, Morgan quickly runs through her to-do list during a wardrobe check, briefly discussing Foundayo with the same actress before being rushed off to stage. 

Morgan and “Life Doesn’t Slow Down” appear on Lilly’s Foundayo partnerships webpage, which gives a brief description of the campaign and includes a direct tag to Morgan’s Instagram account. The comedian is the second celebrity partner to appear on the page after lifestyle guru Martha Stewart, who appeared in Foundayo’s recent “House Rules” campaign. 

Stewart, like Morgan, encourages others to discuss weight management options with their doctor. However, unlike Morgan, her ads come with a disclaimer that Stewart is not taking Foundayo, which attracted some controversy online.

Still, controversial or not, the recognizable face proved successful, with Lilly’s U.S. president Ilya Yuffa attributing a recent uptake in consumer awareness in part to the campaign during an earnings call last month. The exec added that Lilly’s share of new prescriptions in the U.S. oral obesity market is approaching “four out of 10,” which he described as “good progress overall.” 

Foundayo’s third-quarter sales came in at $184 million, falling short of analyst and Wall Street expectations as the drug’s U.S. launch continues to heat up after its April 1 FDA approval. 

Aside from its celebrity marketing push, the company has been looking to grow Foundayo and catch up with obesity rival Novo through expanded access programs. For one, the GLP-1 Bridge program for Medicare Part D patients has seen roughly “seven out of 10” older adult participants using a Lilly medicine since it launched this summer, Yuffa said, highlighting “good growth and uptake of orals and Foundayo” despite most patients in the program opting for an injectable. 

And last week, telehealth giant Hims & Hers struck a deal with Lilly allowing it to offer Foundayo and the company’s injectable Zepbound on its platform. The arrangement gives the “millions of people” who use Hims & Hers a “simple, more direct way to get FDA-approved Lilly medicine at an affordable price if prescribed,” Yuffa said in a statement.

data.title: Summit sheds commercial leaders before ivonescimab FDA decision
data.description:
Summit Therapeutics is gearing up for ivonescimab’s high-stakes FDA decision without its chief commercial officer (CCO) following a quiet shake-up of its launch division.

Beyond the CCO vacancy since August, Summit also eliminated other commercial and marketing leaders responsible for building the launch plan of ivonescimab, Fierce has learned.

After initially denying any layoffs and following multiple inquiries regarding the scope of the cuts, Summit eventually said, “we have not had any broad-based layoffs or reductions in force.”

“As with any organization, less than five employees have been separated from the commercial organization in recent months in the ordinary course of business,” the Summit Therapeutics media team added in an email.

Summit did confirm that Robert LaCaze, its former CCO hired in March 2025, is no longer with the company, leaving all commercial operations reporting to chief operating officer and chief financial officer, Manmeet Soni.

According to a person close to the company, Summit let go of “long-term players in commercial.” These spanned market access to commercial operations and were “the people who did the initial launch planning and moved those plans into maturity,” the person told Fierce.

The departures hit Summit just as the biotech approaches its first FDA decision for ivonescimab, its Akeso-partnered PD-1xVEGF bispecific, by Nov. 14. The company did not respond to Fierce’s question about the size of its commercial team and launch preparations. 

During Summit's second-quarter earnings call in July, shortly before the departure of LaCaze and several commercial team members, Soni said the company was “extensively preparing” for ivonescimab's commercial launch.

“We have already hired all the leadership team with extensive experience with both biotechs and pharma who have multiple launch experiences,” Soni said. “We have market access team in place. We have marketing folks in place. Obviously, when you're talking about the field force, that generally comes a few weeks before the PDUFA date, but yes, we have all the planning and all the work under play.”

Whether the FDA will approve ivonescimab in Summit's application for previously-treated, EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer remains highly uncertain.

Summit’s FDA application was risky after the global HARMONi trial missed its overall survival endpoint, as the agency explicitly requested a statistically significant OS to support a filing. Summit has blamed the failure on immature follow-up in the study's Western population.

According to a new June 2026 data cut-off, the OS hazard ratio in the Western subgroup of 165 patients improved to 0.76, compared to 0.84 at a September 2025 cut-off and 0.98 at the trial’s primary analysis in April 2025.

Related

Summit Therapeutics updates ivonescimab survival data ahead of FDA decision date

As questions swirl around ivonescimab's approvability, Summit's senior leadership proposed foregoing an internal launch meeting, which is commonly set up among biopharma companies to prepare their employees for market readiness, according to the person close to the company.

“What they're doing doesn't make sense for patients. It doesn't make sense for shareholders,” the anonymous source told Fierce. “It doesn't make sense for their own pocketbooks.”

In late September, AstraZeneca made a $2 billion bet in Summit Therapeutics to accelerate the development of ivonescimab in combination with the British pharma's antibody-drug conjugates (ADC).

The newly minted partners will start by testing ivonescimab—which is already approved in China for multiple non-small cell lung cancer indications—with AstraZeneca’s CLDN18.2-directed ADC in gastrointestinal cancers.

data.title: Jeremy Pope joins ViiV in spreading 'PrEP Wisdom'
data.description:
ViiV Healthcare has tapped a new mind for its “PrEP Wisdom” campaign, with Tony Award-winning actor and fashion icon Jeremy Pope joining in on the education and awareness messaging around long-acting injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) options. 

The campaign and its associated website launched in June with “RuPaul’s Drag Race” judge Michelle Visage, who signed on to encourage people to get “PrEP wise” and make informed decisions about long-acting injectable options for HIV prevention. Pope spreads the same message in his new spots, which will reach digital, broadcast, cable, and social platforms, according to ViiV. 

In one 15-second video, Pope is hanging on a brightly colored porch with friends. 

“A good kiki? That’s where the truth comes out,” he says to the camera. “With injectable PrEP options, the truth is there are differences in addition to the dosing schedules.”

Culturally resonant slang terms like “kiki,” which has its roots in Black LGBTQ ballroom culture, are used throughout the campaign. ViiV hopes this kind of language can “cut through the clutter” and prompt its audience to “stop and pause for a minute and pay attention to the messages of the campaign,” head of U.S. ViiV enterprise communications Bithiah Lafont told Fierce in a recent interview. 

HIV disproportionately impacts Black communities in the U.S., according to the CDC, and recent research points to a high unmet need for PrEP in Black men and women. Across the U.S. overall, only 25% of the 2.2 million people who might benefit from PrEP are currently utilizing it, ViiV has said.  

After Gilead Sciences launched Truvada, the first FDA-approved PrEP medication, in 2012, the market was dominated by daily oral options for nearly a decade. That changed in 2021, when ViiV Healthcare's Apretude became the first FDA-approved long-acting injectable PrEP medication. Gilead expanded the market further last year with Yeztugo, a twice-yearly injectable PrEP option.

Related

ViiV Healthcare launches ‘PrEP Wisdom’ campaign to boost awareness of long-acting HIV prevention meds

Much of the buzz around long-acting injectable options has centered on the dosing schedule each can offer, but ViiV and “PrEP Wisdom” look to draw attention to other factors that could play into choice in PrEP. The campaign website encourages people to ask their doctor about potential injection-site reactions, medicine interactions and other considerations that can determine “an option that fits your lifestyle and goals.”  

Pope has been a “great advocate” for the campaign, Lafont said. “Lending his voice and lending his time to this has really boosted our ability to get conversation out to different communities.”

ViiV designed the campaign website with bright colors and playful fonts to make it feel less like a traditional pharma ad, Lafont said. Since its June launch, the site has sparked conversations online and generated social media engagement, supporting the campaign's broader goal of driving behavior change.

“A lot of the change that we’re hoping to see is going to be reflected in those conversations that people are having with their providers,” Lafont explained. “We know that PrEP is one of the best ways for people to prevent HIV, and we also know that the majority of people who could benefit from PrEP are not taking PrEP, and largely that's because either their doctors are not having the conversation or they're not asking their doctors about it.”

She emphasized the importance of informed conversations about PrEP options as the number of long-acting treatments available continues to grow.

As the first company to enter the long-acting injectable PrEP market, ViiV has seen attitudes toward injectable treatments evolve. Lafont pointed to the growing popularity of injectable GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and obesity as one factor contributing to greater acceptance of injectable medicines. Despite that shift, she emphasized that PrEP uptake must increase to make meaningful progress in combating the HIV epidemic.

ViiV, which is majority-owned by GSK and focuses exclusively on HIV, has seen strong growth in its long-acting injectable portfolio. GSK reported that long-acting injectables accounted for 80% of its HIV sales growth in the third quarter, with Apretude generating £403 million ($538.7 million) in sales through the first nine months of 2026. Meanwhile, Gilead's competing Yeztugo brought in $702 million over the same period.

GSK has long maintained that Yeztugo won't dominate the long-acting injectable PrEP market, with executives citing potential tolerability concerns, injection-site nodules and drug interactions as factors that could limit its appeal. The rival drug “definitely won’t be for everyone,” GSK's president of corporate development, David Redfern, said in early 2025.

Still, both companies share a mission to increase U.S. PrEP uptake and normalize conversations around HIV prevention. Gilead recently targeted Hispanic and Latino communities in its “Ahorita Mismo" campaign, while ViiV told prospective HIV treatment or PrEP users to “Do It For Future You” in a recent multichannel campaign.
